hook: The farm boy turned navigator who mapped the Pacific.

pages.x: James Cook was born in 1728 in Yorkshire, the son of a farm labourer. He worked in a shop by the sea, then went to sea on coal ships out of Whitby. At 26 he joined the Royal Navy as a common seaman.
In the Seven Years' War he charted the St Lawrence River so precisely that British ships could carry an army up to Quebec in 1759. His later charts of Newfoundland's coast were used for 200 years.

In 1768 he sailed the Endeavour to Tahiti to watch Venus cross the face of the Sun, then, with secret orders, searched for a southern continent. He charted New Zealand and the east coast of Australia, landing at Botany Bay in 1770.
Scurvy killed more sailors than storms did. Cook made his crews eat sauerkraut, fresh fruit and greens, and kept his ship clean and dry.
pages.fx: On voyages lasting years, almost none of his men died of scurvy, an astonishing feat at the time.

pages.x: On his second voyage he became the first to cross the Antarctic Circle, sailing all the way round the frozen continent without ever seeing it. He found his longitude with a new kind of clock, a copy of John Harrison's marine chronometer.

On his third voyage, searching for a passage around North America, he reached Hawaii. Back there in 1779 to repair a mast, he quarrelled with islanders over a stolen boat, and was killed on the beach at Kealakekua Bay.

Cook mapped more of the Earth than anyone before him, from Canada to Antarctica. His voyages opened the Pacific to European science, trade and settlement, with terrible results for many of its peoples.
pts: Charted New Zealand and eastern Australia
First to cross the Antarctic Circle
Mapped more of the world than anyone before him
